ledger.claim_text: The Boeing 747 was conceived with its distinctive upper cockpit hump specifically to enable straight-in front nose-loading for freight.
ledger.source_title: Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum: Boeing 747 Milestone Aircraft Dossier
ledger.supporting_excerpt_or_notes: Lead designer Joe Sutter and his team placed the cockpit on a second level above the main deck specifically so the nose cone could be hinged upward for roll-on cargo containers.

ledger.claim_text: In the mid-1960s, aviation planners believed supersonic transports (SSTs) like Concorde would render subsonic passenger airliners obsolete within a decade.
ledger.source_title: Boeing Historical Archives: 747 Commercial Transport Program History
ledger.supporting_excerpt_or_notes: Because supersonic transports were predicted to dominate long-haul passenger travel by the 1970s, Boeing designed the 747 to be easily converted into a high-capacity cargo carrier.

ledger.claim_text: Placing the flight deck on the upper deck enabled an unobstructed main deck capable of receiving standard 8-by-8-foot intermodal cargo containers through the swinging nose.
ledger.source_title: 747: Creating the World's First Jumbo Jet and Other Adventures from a Life in Aviation (Joe Sutter)
ledger.supporting_excerpt_or_notes: Pan Am CEO Juan Trippe insisted on carrying two standard 8x8 ft containers side by side; moving the cockpit to an upper pod allowed the nose to open completely without disconnecting control cables.

ledger.claim_text: Aerodynamicist Richard Whitcomb's transonic area rule proved that tapering the upper deck hump into the main fuselage minimized shockwave drag.
ledger.source_title: NASA Technical Reports Server: A Study of the Zero-Lift Drag-Rise Characteristics of Wing-Body Combinations
ledger.publisher: National Advisory Committee for Aeronautics / NASA Langley Research Center
ledger.supporting_excerpt_or_notes: Fairing the cockpit hump smoothly aft satisfied Whitcomb's area rule, smoothing the cross-sectional area progression and reducing transonic wave drag at Mach 0.85.

ledger.claim_text: Boeing constructed the Everett Factory in Washington, the largest building by volume in the world at 472 million cubic feet (13.3 million cubic meters), to assemble the 747.
ledger.source_title: Guinness World Records: Largest Building by Volume
ledger.publisher: Guinness World Records / Boeing Everett Plant
ledger.supporting_excerpt_or_notes: Boeing constructed the Everett factory in 1966 specifically for the 747. It spans 98.3 acres with a continuous volume of 472 million cubic feet, holding the world record.

ledger.claim_text: Overland sonic boom flight restrictions and high fuel consumption grounded commercial supersonic transport expansion, establishing the 747's long-range dominance.
ledger.source_title: Federal Aviation Administration: Overland Supersonic Flight Prohibition History (14 CFR 91.817)
ledger.supporting_excerpt_or_notes: The 1973 FAA overland supersonic ban, coupled with the 1973 oil crisis, terminated the Boeing 2707 SST program and limited Concorde to transatlantic routes, while 747 economy boomed.

ledger.claim_text: Dedicated Boeing 747 freighters continue to transport over half of the world's outsized air cargo due to their unique upward-swinging nose capability.
ledger.supporting_excerpt_or_notes: 747 freighters comprise nearly half of the global large freighter fleet, providing unrivaled front-loading volume for oversize industrial and military cargo.

ledger.claim_text: Over 1,570 Boeing 747 airliners were delivered across a 54-year production run from 1968 to final delivery in January 2023.
ledger.source_title: Boeing Commercial Orders and Deliveries Record / Final 747 Delivery Ceremony
ledger.supporting_excerpt_or_notes: The 1,574th and final Boeing 747 (a 747-8 Freighter) was delivered to Atlas Air on January 31, 2023, concluding 54 years of continuous production.
